projects.name: Benchmarking Soil Moisture Sensors and Irrigation Scheduling Tools in Central Oregon
projects.description: This project evaluates the performance of commonly used soil moisture sensors and irrigation scheduling tools under field conditions in Central Oregon. A neutron probe is used as a reference instrument to benchmark in-situ soil moisture sensors across the root zone, providing an independent assessment of sensor accuracy and reliability. In parallel, the project assesses irrigation recommendations generated by mobile irrigation scheduling tools, including evaluations of how weather data from nearby AgriMet stations influences scheduling performance. By comparing sensor-based measurements, neutron probe observations, and scheduling outputs, the study aims to identify strengths and limitations of current irrigation decision-support tools and improve their application for efficient agricultural water management in semi-arid systems.

projects.name: Field-Scale Validation of Satellite-Based Evapotranspiration Using UAS Thermal Imagery
projects.description:
This project focuses on validating satellite-based evapotranspiration (ET) estimates using high-resolution, field-scale observations. The study integrates ground-based measurements, including soil moisture sensors and a weather station, with drone-mounted thermal imagery collected during satellite overpass periods. These data are used to evaluate the accuracy and performance of satellite-derived ET products under real field conditions.

By synchronizing UAS thermal observations with satellite imagery, the project aims to improve understanding of how satellite ET products perform at the field scale and under varying soil and crop conditions. The results will inform the use of satellite ET tools for agricultural water management, irrigation decision support, and water resource planning in data-sparse and semi-arid environments. This project is a collaboration between OSU and Hydrosat.

projects.name: Lateral 43 Irrigation Modernization & Conservation Planning
projects.description: In partnership with Jefferson County Soil & Water Conservation District (JCSWCD) and funded by Oregon Department of Agriculture ($87,000), COAREC is leading conservation planning for over 40 farming operations covering 7,000 acres that will receive pressurized water when North Unit Irrigation District completes piping of Lateral 43 (construction 2026-2028). This project inventories current irrigation systems, develops farm-specific conservation plans, and identifies opportunities for conversion from flood to sprinkler or drip irrigation and soil health improvements. The project includes water-quality monitoring in Dry Canyon to quantify the runoff-reduction benefits of irrigation modernization. The objectives include providing technical expertise in precision agriculture, soil moisture monitoring, and irrigation efficiency assessment to maximize water-conservation outcomes as this infrastructure investment transforms water delivery for Central Oregon's specialty crop and seed production systems.

location.city: Lateral 43 service area, North Unit Irrigation District, Madras vicinity

projects.name: Evaluating Cost-Effective Conservation Practices to Reduce Nitrate Leaching in the Southern Willamette Valley
projects.description: Groundwater nitrate contamination remains a persistent water-quality challenge in Oregon's Southern Willamette Valley Groundwater Management Area (GWMA), despite more than two decades of voluntary conservation efforts. This project uses measured field data from long-term monitoring sites to evaluate the effectiveness of agricultural conservation practices for reducing nitrate leaching below the root zone while maintaining crop productivity. The study focuses on major regional cropping systems, including grass seed, peppermint, hazelnuts, and wheat. Using the Agricultural Policy Environmental eXtender (APEX) model, the project simulates and compares conservation scenarios such as improved nitrogen fertilizer timing and split applications, winter cover crops, irrigation nitrogen crediting, irrigation system upgrades, and high-frequency low-concentration fertigation. Model results are paired with an economic analysis to identify the most cost-effective practices for each cropping system. Outcomes include science-based recommendations, grower decision-support tools, and guidance to support groundwater protection and sustainable agricultural management in the Willamette Valley.

projects.name: Social Implications of Agricultural AI Enhanced Decision Platform
projects.description:
This project examines how emerging artificial intelligence (AI) decision-support platforms are being used in agricultural water management, and whether they align with the needs, capacities, and concerns of producers, advisors, and water managers. In 2026, we will conduct interviews and surveys with agricultural producers and professionals across Oregon to assess current use, perceptions, and barriers related to AI-enabled tools for irrigation, drought response, and water conservation.

The project identifies social, institutional, and equity-related challenges to AI adoption while documenting stakeholder needs and priorities for future tool development. Findings will inform the improvement of more transparent, inclusive, and trusted AI decision-support platforms that support climate-resilient and socially responsible water management.

projects.name: Conservation Practice Adoption and Farm Financial Support in Oregon
projects.description: This project investigates how farm financial programs, such as crop insurance, operating loans, and conservation cost-share programs, shape agricultural producers' decisions related to soil and water conservation and land management in wheat and livestock production in Oregon. Using interviews with farmers and agricultural professionals, the study examines how financial incentives, risk management tools, and advisory relationships relate to the adoption of soil and water conservation practices. The findings will help inform the design of agricultural financial and conservation policies by clarifying how existing programs shape producers' soil and water management decisions.

projects.name: Social Network Analysis of Oregon Agricultural and Natural Resource Organizations
projects.description:
This project maps and analyzes collaboration networks among agricultural and natural resource organizations in Oregon to understand how partnerships and information flow across the system. Using social network analysis, the project examines which organizations act as key connectors and where gaps or silos may limit coordination.

The results help identify opportunities to strengthen cross-sector collaboration, improve outreach to producers, and enhance the effectiveness of water-related programs by leveraging existing institutional networks.

projects.name: Statewide Soil Moisture Sensing (SMS) and Evapotranspiration (ET) Project
projects.description:
This project develops and deploys a statewide, cost-effective soil moisture and evapotranspiration (ET) monitoring network to improve irrigation decision-making across Oregon's diverse agricultural regions. Originally proposed to design and field-test a low-cost soil moisture sensing system (CE-SMS) at Oregon's Branch Experiment Stations (BES), the project has expanded in scope to integrate plant- and atmosphere-based measurements, irrigation automation, and centralized data access platforms. Together, these components support more precise irrigation scheduling, water conservation, and energy efficiency while maintaining crop productivity.

The CE-SMS network uses open-source electronics, Watermark soil water potential sensors, cellular connectivity, and solar power to enable scalable, field-ready monitoring. Fully operational CE-SMS systems are now deployed at North Willamette Research and Extension Center (NWREC), Southern Oregon Research and Extension Center (SOREC), and the Malheur Experiment Station (MES), supporting multiple crops and irrigation systems. As the project evolved, LI-COR LI-710 evapotranspiration sensors were incorporated across Oregon in collaboration with growers, allowing direct measurement of crop water use and cross-comparison with soil moisture-based irrigation thresholds. The project now integrates soil moisture data, ET measurements, irrigation automation, and cloud-based dashboards into a unified framework that supports both research and Extension, and lays the foundation for broader on-farm adoption in future phases.

projects.name: Soil Sensor Testing Bed for Evaluation and Calibration of Irrigation Technologies
projects.description:
This project is developing an indoor irrigation testing bed designed to advance precision irrigation management, sensor evaluation, and Extension outreach. The testbed consists of multiple soil sections spanning a range of textures—from sandy to clay soils—instrumented with commercially available soil moisture sensors and computer-controlled drip irrigation. By isolating soil processes from plant and atmospheric effects, the system enables controlled, repeatable testing across contrasting soil types representative of Oregon production systems.

The testing bed serves three primary functions: (1) benchmarking soil moisture sensor performance across soil textures to support reliable irrigation decisions; (2) developing and validating modeling, forecasting, and control algorithms that automatically adjust irrigation based on soil conditions; and (3) providing a highly visual Extension demonstration platform. Transparent acrylic panels allow direct observation of water movement through soil profiles, making subsurface processes intuitive and accessible for growers, students, and technical audiences. Together, this work supports more efficient water use and accelerates the adoption of data-driven irrigation management practices. This project is a collaboration with AgAID (https://agaid.org/soil-water-content-prediction)

projects.name: Evaluating Crop Evapotranspiration, Soil Moisture, and Cover Crop Effects in Willamette Valley Hazelnut Orchards
projects.description:
This project quantifies the water requirements of hazelnut orchards in the Willamette Valley and evaluates how orchard floor management—bare ground, grass, and clover cover crops—influences crop evapotranspiration (ETc), soil moisture availability, and indicators of crop water stress. Sixteen hazelnut orchard plots distributed across the valley represent these ground-cover treatments, enabling comparisons across sites with similar soils and climatic conditions.

To address crop water use directly, the study evaluates and compares ETc estimates derived from multiple methods, including in-situ meteorological and flux-based measurements, nearby AgriMet weather stations, and satellite-based ET products. Continuous soil moisture monitoring at multiple depths captures how cover crops affect root-zone water availability, while advanced imaging technologies—such as multispectral vegetation indices (e.g., NDVI) and thermal imagery—are used to assess canopy condition and plant water stress. By integrating atmospheric demand, soil moisture dynamics, and plant response, the project examines how cover crops alter the relationships among ETc, available soil water, and crop stress throughout the growing season. The results provide field-based evidence to support irrigation management decisions in hazelnut orchards under different ground-cover strategies.

projects.name: Evaluating Low-Cost OPEnS Lab Dendrometers for Plant-Based Irrigation Management in Hazelnuts and Blueberries
projects.description:
This project evaluates the use of dendrometers to monitor plant water status in hazelnut orchards and blueberry fields as part of ARF-supported irrigation research. Dendrometers provide continuous measurements of stem or trunk diameter variation, which reflect short-term plant hydration dynamics and longer-term growth responses to irrigation and atmospheric demand. The objective is to assess when and how dendrometer signals provide actionable information for irrigation management in perennial specialty crops.

Dendrometer measurements are evaluated alongside soil moisture, evapotranspiration (ET), vapor pressure deficit (VPD), and traditional indicators of plant water status across contrasting irrigation treatments and phenological stages. By comparing dendrometer-derived metrics between hazelnuts and blueberries, the project examines species-specific sensitivity, environmental drivers, and practical limitations of plant-based sensing. Results help define the role of dendrometers within multi-sensor irrigation frameworks and support guidance on their appropriate use for water-stress detection and irrigation decision-making.
